headline: The Tulip That Wasn't: Why Duration Doesn't Disprove Bubbles
lede: The standard rejoinder to Bitcoin skeptics — "tulips only lasted months, Bitcoin has survived sixteen years" — rests on a comparison that flatters both sides less than it appears. The tulip story itself turns out to be largely myth, and the duration argument, while seductive, proves less than its champions think.
body:
Every asset that appreciates sharply acquires, sooner or later, its tulip metaphor. The reference is meant to sting: in the winter of 1636–37, Dutch speculators allegedly bid a single bulb of the coveted *Semper Augustus* variety to the price of a canal-side Amsterdam townhouse, only for the whole trade to collapse in a matter of weeks and ruin thousands. The image is irresistible — flowers as securities, a nation undone by horticulture. There is just one problem, and it is rather large: the story is not quite true.

The tulip mania's popular narrative was built largely on a single source. In 1841, the Scottish journalist Charles Mackay published *Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds*, a rollicking catalogue of human folly that devoted its opening chapters to the tulip trade, the South Sea Bubble, and the Mississippi Company. Mackay's account was vivid, moralistic, and, as subsequent historians have established, substantially plagiarised from earlier German pamphlets that were themselves anti-speculation propaganda, not sober reporting. The historian Anne Goldgar, whose 2008 book *Tulipmania: Money, Honor, and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age* is the most thorough archival examination of the episode, found that she could not locate a single verifiable case of anyone who was bankrupted by the crash. The trade, she concluded, was confined to a fairly small network of merchants and skilled craftsmen in a handful of Dutch cities. The most expensive receipts she could document were for 5,000 guilders — the price of a modest house, not a grand one — and fewer than three dozen people paid more than 300 guilders, roughly a craftsman's annual wage, for any bulb. The economic carnage that has made tulip mania a byword for irrational excess appears, on inspection, to be largely a moralist's invention amplified by two centuries of retelling.

What Goldgar did find was something more psychologically interesting: a crisis of trust rather than capital. Because tulip contracts were typically settled in spring, when bulbs could be dug up and inspected, the entire trade rested on personal honour and networks of credit. When prices collapsed in February 1637 — triggered, by one account, by an auctioneer in Haarlem who found no buyers even after repeatedly lowering his asking price — what broke was not a financial system but a social one. Buyers refused to honour contracts; reputations were destroyed; relationships ended. The economist Peter Garber, another revisionist, has gone further, suggesting that much of the late-stage common-bulb trading was essentially a winter tavern game played by a population in the grip of a plague year, not a sophisticated futures market. The genuine speculative excess, such as it was, lasted perhaps six weeks.

Against this backdrop, the duration argument beloved of Bitcoin advocates takes on a different complexion. Noah Kaufman, an emergency physician and Bitcoin educator, makes the point that bubbles pop quickly whereas Bitcoin has persisted for fifteen-plus years through repeated crashes of 70–90 percent and has still reached new all-time highs — trading above $110,000 in 2025 after spot exchange-traded funds were approved in the United States. The argument has real force: no classical bubble has survived multiple near-total drawdowns and still produced new peaks. Tulip prices, after all, never recovered. But "duration does not equal fundamentals" cuts both ways. Japan's Nikkei index took thirty-four years to return to its 1989 peak. The argument from longevity is a necessary condition for ruling out the simplest bubble narrative, not a sufficient one for ruling out subtler versions.

What the comparison genuinely does illuminate is the asymmetry in the emotional weight the two episodes carry. The tulip metaphor works rhetorically because it conjures an image of blind collective madness, of a society that briefly lost its mind over flowers. That image is emotionally compelling precisely because it is so extreme — and it is so extreme, Goldgar's work suggests, because it was confected for polemical purposes in the seventeenth century and has been laundered through Mackay's prose into economic orthodoxy. Bitcoin skeptics who reach for the tulip comparison are borrowing the moral force of a cautionary tale that, on close examination, does not quite describe what they think it describes. Conversely, Bitcoin advocates who cite duration as dispositive proof of value are doing something equally convenient: treating survival as proof of soundness, when what survival actually demonstrates is resilience — a related but distinct quality.

The honest position sits somewhere in the gap between the two rhetorical moves. Bitcoin has properties — fixed supply, programmable settlement, global transferability without a central counterparty — that tulip bulbs self-evidently lacked. It has also displayed, on multiple occasions, the price dynamics that define a speculative mania: parabolic appreciation, narrative-driven retail influx, and crashes that wiped out the majority of paper gains within months. Whether those dynamics reflect a market still discovering the price of a genuinely novel asset or a recurring bubble on a long plateau is a question that neither the tulip comparison nor the duration counter-argument can settle. What Goldgar's scholarship at least establishes is that the canonical warning story, the one that haunts every crypto dinner-table debate, was always more parable than history.

concepts.definition: A speculative episode in the Dutch Republic (1634–1637) during which contract prices for certain rare tulip bulbs rose sharply before collapsing in February 1637. Long cited as history's first great financial bubble, the episode has been substantially revised by modern historians who found it was smaller in scale, shorter in duration, and far less economically devastating than Charles Mackay's 1841 popularisation suggested.

A sustained period in which an asset's market price far exceeds any reasonable estimate of its fundamental value, typically characterised by rapid price appreciation, speculative buying driven more by expected resale profit than intrinsic utility, and an eventual sharp correction. The term is contested because identifying a bubble in real time requires knowing the 'true' fundamental value — a notoriously difficult judgment.

An agreement to buy or sell a specified asset at a predetermined price on a future date. In the tulip trade, most bulbs were contracted for future delivery while still in the ground; this meant that during the mania, enormous notional prices were being set for goods that did not yet physically exist, and that 'money had not changed hands' — which partly explains why the crash, though socially traumatic, produced relatively few documented bankruptcies.

books.title: Tulipmania: Money, Honor, and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age
books.author: Anne Goldgar
books.note: The definitive revisionist account of the 1637 episode, based on extensive archival research in Dutch notarial records. Goldgar argues the bubble was geographically confined, involved a small network of participants, caused no documented bankruptcies, and is best understood as a crisis of social trust rather than a financial catastrophe. Published by University of Chicago Press, 2008.

books.title: Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds
books.author: Charles Mackay
books.note: The 1841 text responsible for embedding the dramatic tulip mania narrative into popular consciousness. Modern historians including Goldgar and Peter Garber have shown Mackay plagiarised much of his account from earlier German pamphlets that were themselves anti-speculation propaganda rather than factual reporting.

fact_check: The claim that no documented bankruptcy resulted from the tulip crash is supported by Goldgar's archival research and is also noted in the Wikipedia article on tulip mania. The peak price of 5,000 guilders for certain bulbs, and the figure of fewer than 37 (some sources say 'fewer than half a dozen' for serious financial difficulty) people paying above 300 guilders, come from Goldgar's primary research as reported across multiple secondary sources. The February 1637 collapse date and the Haarlem auctioneer episode are well-attested in the historical record. Bitcoin's 2025 price above $110,000 following spot ETF approvals is consistent with multiple sources including OANDA's price history. The Nikkei 34-year return-to-peak figure is accurate: the index peaked in December 1989 and did not sustainably exceed that level until 2024. Kaufman is an emergency physician and Bitcoin author — this is confirmed by KevinMD.com podcast listings and his Apple Podcasts appearances.
